paras: The attempted lynching at Gadsden, Alabama, took place on a Sunday night in late July 1905, when a mob of about 300 people marched on the Gadsden jail to seize six Black prisoners charged with the rape and murder of a white widow, Mrs. S. J. Smith. The mob dispersed after a congressman, the militia commander and the sheriff appealed to it.

According to a Montgomery dispatch, early on a Sunday Vance Gardner reported finding Mrs. Smith's body in roadside bushes three-quarters of a mile from Gadsden, the crime having been committed the night before. Six Black people were then jailed on the charge: Gardner, William Johnson, Ed (or E. D.) Johnson, Bud Richardson, Jefferson Alford and Fannie Mayo, the one woman among them.

That evening a crowd of some 300 gathered on Broad Street and later marched on the jail, demanding that the doors be opened; one young man had "the rope ready to swing Vance Gardner." At ten o'clock the sheriff telegraphed the governor that his jail was "threatened by a mob," and the governor placed the Gadsden company of state troops at his disposal. After Congressman John L. Burnett, the militia commander, Sheriff Chandler and others appealed to the crowd, it dispersed.
None of the prisoners is reported harmed, and no report of an inquest or a trial of the six was found.

The Logan Republican of Utah ran the Montgomery wire on 2 August under "WHITE WOMAN ASSAULTED. Six Negroes Implicated in the Assault and Murder," leading with the alleged crime. The Crook County Monitor of Sundance, Wyoming, printed an earlier, midnight version on 18 August as "MILITIA CALLED OUT. Alabama Negroes in Danger of Being Lynched," with the outcome still unknown. Both called the prisoners "negroes" and presented the charges as charges; no Black-press account was found.
The Utah paper named the militia commander "Lieutenant A. R. Brindley" and the Wyoming paper "Capt. L. Braney," probably the same officer garbled in transmission.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Gadsden, Alabama (1905)
bases: A mob of about 300 gathered at the Gadsden jail and threatened to lynch six jailed Black prisoners accused of rape and murder, but dispersed without taking them (A1, A2).
A mob of 300 sought to take accused prisoners from jail to lynch them in reprisal for an alleged rape and murder, but no one was killed; the mob dispersed after appeals (A1, A2).

Both reports are versions of the same Montgomery wire story built on the sheriff's telegram and the governor's office, one filed at midnight (A2) and one after the mob dispersed (A1); no local Alabama or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Wire report from Montgomery, later version
accounts.gist: Reports that the troops were ordered out and that the mob dispersed after appeals by a congressman, the militia lieutenant and the sheriff, and adds details of the alleged crime.

framing.detail: The Utah paper led with the alleged crime, 'WHITE WOMAN ASSAULTED. Six Negroes Implicated', and stated the charges as charges.
The Wyoming weekly framed the story around the danger to the prisoners, 'Alabama Negroes in Danger of Being Lynched', among other national briefs.

info: A Sunday night shortly before 2 August 1905, most likely 30 July 1905 (inferred from A1's publication date); A2, printed 18 August, gives only 'Sunday night'.
The jail at Gadsden, Alabama; the crowd first gathered on Broad Street.

Six Black prisoners in the Gadsden jail, five men and one woman: Vance Gardner, William Johnson, Ed (E. D.) Johnson, Bud Richardson (Richarson), Jefferson Alford and Fannie Mayo; none was harmed in the reports.

Charged with the rape and murder of Mrs. S. J. Smith, a white widow, whose body was found early Sunday in bushes by the roadside three-quarters of a mile from Gadsden; the crime was said to have been committed Saturday night.
A mob gathered in Gadsden; no members were named.
The mob dispersed after the appeals; no one was lynched. A2, an earlier version, says nothing further was known at midnight.
